title: The Barrow Roll of Hollin
author: begun by Orm Hollin, Barrow Reeve, and continued in his hand for rather longer than that
body:
# The Barrow Roll of Hollin

*Kept in the Bell Cist. Read at the turn of each season, aloud, by the Reeve.*

---

**Orm Hollin**, Reeve of this ground, who dug the first cist and lay down in the fourth.

**Maud Hollin**, his wife, buried with her own shears and a loaf, the loaf being custom and the shears being hers.

**Ansel Hollin**, seven years, buried with a wooden bell.

*(Here forty-one lines, each a name, each with the tool it went down holding: a billhook, a shepherd's crook, three ladles, a mason's square, a bee-skep, an eel-knife brought up from the Mere, a fiddle.)*

---

## The second hand, which is the same hand

**Larkstead.** Fourteen hearths. The whole village, in the winter of 993, brought down the lane on carts by nobody, because there was nobody left in Larkstead to bring them. I have written the fourteen names I could find cut on their doorsteps. I have written *and others* under them, and I am ashamed of the line and I will not scratch it out.

**Gosford.** Nine hearths. Not here. Not anywhere. I walked it in 981 and again in 982 and there is a green and a lane and no ground that has been opened.

---

## What a Reeve is for

A Warden's Roll says a place is still under its name. This roll says a person is still under this ground. They are the same work and the Rest has forgotten that it split off from us, and I have stopped writing letters about it.

The reading is the whole of the office. Not the digging; anybody can dig. A hundred and forty names at the turn of a season takes a little over forty minutes and it must be done aloud, because a name read in the head is a name thought about, and thinking about a thing is not the same as saying it where the air can carry it.

I am past being able to say who has been reading them lately. I know that they are read. I know that the bell in this cist is the only warm thing in the ground and that it was hung by somebody who understood what warmth is for.

If you have this roll in your hands and you are breathing, then I have stopped, and forty minutes of your season belongs to a hundred and forty people who are not in a position to ask.

title: The Figures: a held breath, nightly, forty-one years
author: Ismay Ondrael, Sayer of the Breath, who is the instrument and says so on the first page
body:
# The Figures

*Four columns: the date, the hour, the glass-count, the room. Kept nightly since Y.T. 1002. The fourth column was added in the ninth year, for reasons given below.*

---

## The first page, written last

If the world is being breathed in, breath itself may be shortening, and nobody has ever taken the measurement. So: one glass, one set of lungs, one hour of an evening, for as long as I last.

The result, stated plainly and not published: **it is shorter.** By rather more than a woman going from three years old to forty-four should account for. Not enough to be certain. Certainly enough to be frightening.

I have not published it and I have been asked twice why not, and the answer is the fourth column.

## The fourth column

In the ninth year I noticed that the figure was low in my own cell and high in the refectory, and that I had been taking it in my own cell for nine years. So I began to write down the room.

The figure is longest in a warm room with people talking in it. It is shortest in a cold room by myself. The difference between those two is larger than the difference between me at thirty and me at forty-four.

This is a ruinous result for my own account and I have set it down in the middle of my own book. If the Breath were taking the world's air, the room would not matter. The room matters more than the year.

## Why the instrument cannot publish

Because the instrument is frightened, and a frightened instrument reads low, and I cannot subtract my own fear from a column of my own figures.

What is wanted is somebody young and unfrightened to take the same glass into a warm room and a cold one and write the figures in their own hand, so that the result is not mine. I have said this in three lectures. Nobody has offered.

*(Below, in a second and much newer hand, the figures from a warm inn on a market night and from a bell-hall under a city, twenty paces from running water, with nobody talking.)*

title: Charter Entry 998/xi: the Building of the Row Strongroom
author: the Tallymen of Tollmere; this copy made on Lantern Row by Cassa Binder, binder, who copies everything
body:
# Charter Entry 998/xi

*Entered at the Guild Hall, Tollmere, in the eleventh month of Y.T. 998. Copied fair. Nothing omitted.*

---

**Item.** That a strongroom be built at the foot of Lantern Row for the keeping of the Guild's books, the Ledger of Prices among them, the present press in the tally-house being neither dry nor sole-keyed.

**Item.** Paid to Sorrel Lathe, mason, for footings cut to a depth of eleven feet: two hundred and forty marks. *Note in the margin: the mason asked for nine feet and was required to cut eleven, and said that at eleven he would strike the black stone, and did.*

**Item.** Paid for iron, door, frame, and a lock of three wards: one hundred and ninety marks.

**Item.** Of the walls. Three walls of coursed limestone, eighteen inches, lime-washed within.

**Item.** Of the fourth wall. *The east wall being already standing, of a fused black stone of the Builders, curved, and of no known thickness, it was thought a saving to course the new walls to it rather than raise a fourth. The mason objected that a wall you did not build is a wall you do not know. The Guild replied that a wall the Builders made is a better wall than a wall Sorrel Lathe makes, at which the mason was pleased and withdrew the objection.*

**Item.** Paid to the mason, for his objection withdrawn: nothing.

---

*(In Cassa Binder's own hand, at the foot of the last leaf:)*

I have copied this entry eleven times in nine years, for clerks, for a Sayer, and twice for men who did not give a reason. Nobody has ever asked me the question, so I will write it here and charge nobody for it.

The Guild built its strongroom against the outside of a curved black wall eleven feet down at the foot of Lantern Row. There is exactly one curved black Oroth thing eleven feet under that end of the city and it is not a wall. It is a bell. And people live in it.

title: The Ledger of Prices
author: eleven stewards of the Tallymen of Tollmere, Y.T. 952 to the present, each of them tidy
body:
# The Ledger of Prices

*The Guild's book of what the law of Tollmere has cost and who paid it. Opened Y.T. 952. Not posted.*

---

## What is in it

Every fine levied by the paid watch, with the name, the offence, the figure, and a fourth column headed **regard**, in which the steward of the day has written what the payer was owed or owing, socially, at the time.

That fourth column is the whole book. Without it this is a tax roll and the Guild would nail it to the charter-board tomorrow, as it nails up everything else, with justified pride.

## A page, as an example. Y.T. 1041, the ninth month.

| name | offence | figure | regard |
|---|---|---|---|
| T. Ashdown, carter, of Merrowby | barrow standing in the Row | 4 | *chartered trade; brings the Vale's iron; the Guild wants him next spring* |
| J. Wick, fisher, of Gullhithe | barrow standing in the Row | 40 | *unchartered; sells direct; the fishmongers have asked twice* |
| A Sayer of the Circle, unnamed here | affray at the Long Stride | 0 | *the Spire pays no fines and we do not ask; noted for the record* |
| M. Brambling, baker, of Merrowby | short weight, one loaf | 2 | *the loaf was a gift and the watchman a fool; remitted; the watchman spoken to* |

## The three sentences the Guild would rather not have written down

**952, the first steward.** *A price openly set is a price that may be argued with. That is the Charter's virtue and it is the reason we write down what we take.*

**998, the fourth steward.** *It is observed that where regard is high the figure is low, and that this is not corruption but the market in standing, which is a real market and ought to be recorded as one.*

**1043, the eleventh steward, in Orrin Quill's hand.** *I have totalled the fourth column for ninety-one years. Being thought well of in this city is worth, on the average, thirty-one marks in the pound. I do not know what to do with that figure and I have shown it to nobody, and I post everything.*

title: The Chapter Roll of Pilgrim's Ash
author: the Tolling Order; kept by whoever has the watch, and read aloud at the turn of it
body:
# The Chapter Roll

*Who is standing the watch. Read at the turn of the watch, aloud, both sides. The Vigil Book is for pilgrims; this is ours.*

---

## Standing

**Cadwen Ash**, Toll-Knight, nineteen years, the night watch at the ring.

**Toren Ash**, Toll-Knight, four years, the day watch.

*(Seven more, with their years and their watches. Then, without any change of ink or heading:)*

**Auvrey Tull**, Sister, the north walk. *Went out to the fourth colossus on a still night in 1024 and has not come back to the chapter-house. The watch is hers until she does.*

**Ossel**, smith's daughter, of Gullhithe, the forge and the west walk. *Autumn of 1019. Went to bring in a bell-bearer's clapper and did not. It is her quench we use. The watch is hers.*

**Halloran Ash**, Bell-Sworn, the glass falls. *1031.*

*(Eight more like them. Eleven in all.)*

---

## The rule of the standing side

A name comes off the standing side when the Order knows the knight has ended. Not when the knight has not come back; not after a year; not after nine. When the Order **knows**.

The Order has never known. Nobody has ever gone out to the walks and looked, because looking would mean finding, and finding would mean writing a name on the other side of this book, and the other side of this book has four names on it in ninety years and three of those died in their cots at the chapter-house with somebody holding their hand.

So eleven knights are read out every night as standing the watch, and they are standing it, after a fashion, in grey plate, on their own walks, and the bells still go, and the Order counts them.

*(At the foot, in Cadwen Ash's hand:)*

I have read Ossel's name out four thousand times. I would like it understood by whoever reads this after me that I know exactly what I am doing, and that the alternative is a book with eleven lines crossed out in it, and that I have not yet been able to decide which of those two books is the honest one. I am not stalling. I am nineteen years into the question.
